item.title: Barclays is latest to redirect spending toward AI as it trims its workforce
item.description: The cost of building out the infrastructure needed to satisfy booming demand for artificial intelligence is changing the way major companies allocate resources.
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: The cost of building out the infrastructure needed to satisfy booming demand for artificial intelligence is changing the way major companies allocate resources. That can mean an end to some jobs once done by humans. Yet in many cases it means repurposing money once spent on workers so that more capital can be devoted to boosting AI capabilities. Just how much money is being spent on AI is a hot topic as fears of a bubble in the sector grow, but the potential impact on workers in some sectors is clear. Here’s a look at some of the companies that have announced layoffs or hiring reductions this year that are tied in some way to massive spending on AI. Barclays The U.K. bank and financial services company revealed in a quarterly financial report this week that it is looking to cut 5,000 jobs, or about five per cent of its workforce. The company said that it was seeking “organisational simplification and technology change efficiency driven by AI.” Approximately 60 per cent of the cuts will be from support functions, including developers. Financial institutions are among the most active in deploying AI, in many cases at the expense of workers. Norway’s DNB and Commerzbank in Germany have also announced job cuts in parallel with a push into AI. Kroger Kroger said last week that it will lay off 3,000 corporate employees over the next three years as the national grocery chain ramps up its use of artificial intelligence. “Technology is reshaping what’s possible,” CEO Greg Foran wrote in a memo to employees. “The way work gets done is changing across every industry; we must adapt and take advantage of technology. We need to adopt capabilities, reduce duplicative work and look closely at where work is best fit to be done.” Kroger last month outlined its AI strategy, meant “to improve the customer experience, make work easier for associates and produce better business outcomes.” The Cincinnati company is the largest standalone U.S. supermarket chain with 409,000 employees and more than 2,700 stores operating under various brands, including Ralphs, King Soopers, Smith’s and Fred Meyer. Meta The company that runs Facebook and Instagram said it would lay off about 8,000 workers, or about 10 per cent of its workforce, as it continues to ramp up spending on artificial intelligence infrastructure and highly paid AI-expert hires. The company said in April that it was making the cuts for the sake of efficiency and to allow new investments in parts of its business, as first reported by Bloomberg, which also said the company will leave about 6,000 jobs unfilled. Meta had already warned investors that its 2026 expenses will grow significantly — to as much as US$169 billion — driven by infrastructure costs and employee compensation, particularly for the artificial intelligence experts it’s been hiring. Microsoft Software giant Microsoft is offering voluntary buyouts to thousands of its U.S. employees. The company planned to make the offers in early May to about 8,750 people, or 7 per cent of its U.S. workforce, according to two people familiar with the plan who were not authorized to speak about it publicly. Microsoft has spent billions of dollars operating an ever-expanding global network of data centres powering cloud computing services, AI systems and its own suite of productivity tools, including the AI assistant Copilot. Standard Chartered The U.K.-based bank is planning to cut more than 15 per cent of its back office employees by 2030. Standard Chartered said in May that it was “scaling practical uses of automation, advanced analytics and artificial intelligence to streamline processes, improve decision‑making and enhance both client service and internal efficiency.” Coinbase The cryptocurrency trading platform is cutting approximately 14 per cent of its workforce partly due to AI. In a blog post, CEO Brian Armstrong said that AI was changing the way that Coinbase worked. “Over the past year, I’ve watched engineers use AI to ship in days what used to take a team weeks,” he wrote. “Non-technical teams are now shipping production code and many of our workflows are being automated. The pace of what’s possible with a small, focused team has changed dramatically, and it’s accelerating every day.” Armstrong said that the company needed to take action. “We are adjusting early and deliberately to rebuild Coinbase to be lean, fast, and AI-native,” he wrote. Pinterest Pinterest announced in January that it planned to lay off under 15 per cent of its workforce as part of a broader restructuring as the image-sharing platform pivots more of its money to artificial intelligence. In a securities filing, the company said that it was making the cuts to support “transformation initiatives” — which include reallocating resources to AI-focused roles and prioritizing AI-powered products. It said it was also working to reshape its “sales and go-to-market approach.” Snap The owner of social media platform Snapchat is eliminating about 16 per cent of its global workforce, or about 1,000 jobs. “The headcount reduction is designed to further streamline our operations and reallocate resources toward our highest-priority initiatives, leveraging increased operational efficiencies to accelerate our path toward net-income profitability,” the company said in a regulatory filing. CEO Evan Spiegel said in a letter to staff in April that another 300 open roles would not be filled. Block Financial technology company Block is laying off more than 4,000 of its 10,000 plus employees, reconfiguring to capitalize on its use of artificial intelligence. “The core thesis is simple. Intelligence tools have changed what it means to build and run a company,” Jack Dorsey said in a letter to shareholders in Block, the parent company to online payment platforms such as Square and Cash App. “A significantly smaller team, using the tools we’re building, can do more and do it better,” he said. Dorsey’s comments explicitly naming AI as a key driver behind the decision were also posted on X, or Twitter, a company he co-founded. The announcement has sent shares of the company sharply higher this year, up 19 per cent, reversing a 12 per cent decline in the previous year. --- Michelle Chapman, The Associated Press

item.title: Rogers seeks to offset hit from CRTC fee ban as wireless service revenue dips in Q3
item.description: Rogers Communications Inc. says it is seeking to offset the hit it has taken from the CRTC’s recent ban on telecommunications carriers charging certain administrative fees.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: TORONTO — Rogers Communications Inc. says it is seeking to offset the hit it has taken from the CRTC’s recent ban on telecommunications carriers charging certain administrative fees. While Rogers reported a year-over-year increase in overall revenue during its most recent quarter, primarily due to growth in its media division, the company said wireless service revenue decreased one per cent. During its third quarter, Rogers’ mobile phone average monthly revenue per user was $55.22, down from $56.70 in the same quarter of the prior year. Chief financial officer Glenn Brandt said the “largest impact” to that closely watched figure came from the CRTC’s move in June to prohibit telecoms from charging customers when they activate, change or cancel plans. “The purpose of those setup fees was exactly that — to offset costs of account changes or new accounts coming on,” Brandt told analysts on a conference call Friday. “The charge disappeared (due to) the CRTC decision. The costs don’t.” He said Rogers put in place some “early initiatives” during the quarter to recover some of those costs, but “there’s still more work to do.” “We’re now moving back to finding alternatives for covering those costs, shipping costs, for example … so that effort remains ongoing.” The CRTC has said the new rules are meant to make it easier for customers to switch internet and cellphone plans without having to worry about unexpected charges. The regulator is in the midst of a review into whether Rogers, along with rivals Bell Canada and Telus Corp., violated the ban by introducing new fees around the time it took effect. It said Rogers began charging customers a $40 device setup fee, $25 shipping charge, and an unspecified SIM card fee in mid-June that “would not appear” to qualify for an exemption under the rules for optional services or products that consumers consent to purchase. Rogers has argued the device setup fee is related to an optional purchase. It also said the shipping and SIM fees were not new, and that the latter is only charged when a customer replaces a lost or damaged SIM, rather than at activation. Overall, the quarter saw a “less active telecom market,” said Rogers president and CEO Tony Staffieri said, as the company reported a profit attributable to shareholders of $482 million. “In wireless, we stayed focused on financials versus chasing subscriber volume in what is typically a busy back-to-school quarter,” he told analysts. The company reported 17,000 total mobile phone net subscriber additions, including 6,000 postpaid — those who pay a monthly bill for their wireless services after charges have accumulated. That was down from 62,000 postpaid additions in the same quarter last year. Rogers’ monthly churn — a measure of those who cancelled their service — for net postpaid mobile subscribers was 1.03 per cent, up from 0.99 per cent during its previous third quarter. Retail internet net additions totalled 10,000, down from 29,000 a year earlier. The company said its profit amounted to 88 cents per diluted share for the quarter ended Sept. 30. The result compared with a profit of $5.71 billion or $10.54 per diluted share a year ago when it saw a $5-billion non-cash gain related to its stake in Maple Leaf Sports & Entertainment and $151-million gain on the redemption of long-term debt. On an adjusted basis, Rogers said it earned $704 million in net income, or $1.29 per diluted share in its latest quarter, down from an adjusted profit of $1.37 per diluted share a year ago. Revenue totalled $5.44 billion, up from $5.35 billion in the same quarter last year. “Financial results were in line with our forecast while subscriber growth was a little lighter than our forecast,” said RBC analyst Drew McReynolds in a note. “We view the results as largely neutral for the shares at current levels.” Earlier this month, Rogers completed its $4.35-billion purchase of the remaining 25 per cent stake in MLSE it did not already hold, giving it complete ownership of the sports conglomerate that includes the Maple Leafs, Raptors, Toronto FC and Argonauts. Staffieri reiterated Rogers’ plan to sell a minority interest in its consolidated sports, media and entertainment portfolio to third-party investors, adding he remains “bullish about our plan to unlock shareholder value and drive long-term growth.” Rogers is targeting the first half of 2027 to close that minority interest sale. “Investor interest in these assets is substantial as sports franchise valuations continue to rise,” Staffieri said. This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 23, 2026. By Sammy Hudes BNN Bloomberg, CTV News and CP24 are owned by Bell Media, which is a division of BCE.

item.title: When should you start collecting CPP and OAS?: Stan Wong
item.description: Who would turn down a 42 per cent pay raise? That is effectively the choice facing Canadians deciding when to collect their Canada Pension Plan (CPP).
item.content:encoded:
Who would turn down a 42 per cent pay raise? That is effectively the choice facing Canadians deciding when to collect their Canada Pension Plan (CPP). Waiting until 70 rather than starting at 65 increases monthly payments by 42 per cent. The catch? Five years without collecting a penny.

Clients frequently ask me whether they should begin collecting CPP as early as age 60, wait until 65 or defer until 70, and when they should start Old Age Security (OAS). Many instinctively favour taking the money early. But the better question is how these decisions fit into their overall financial plan. Do you actually need the income? Consider two retirees, both aged 65. One has a workplace pension, substantial investments, and no immediate need for additional income. Deferring CPP could strengthen financial security later. The other relies on investment withdrawals to pay everyday expenses. Collecting earlier might reduce the need to sell investments during a market downturn. The same pension rules can produce very different answers. A comprehensive financial plan can project cash flow, compare investment withdrawals, and identify the trade-offs of waiting, including forgone returns and potential taxes. Taxes can change the calculation Both CPP and OAS are taxable, but only OAS faces an income-tested recovery tax, commonly called the clawback. For the 2026 income year, the OAS clawback starts above $95,323 in individual net income, with 15 cents recovered for each additional dollar. This generally affects recoveries from July 2027 through June 2028. At a net income of $120,000, including OAS, roughly $3,700 would be recovered. For recipients aged 65 to 74, the benefit can be fully clawed back at $155,320. CPP has no comparable clawback, although receiving it can increase taxable income and, consequently, OAS repayments. The broader retirement income picture is crucial: someone retiring before mandatory withdrawals from a registered retirement income fund (RRIF) begin may benefit from drawing down savings in a registered retirement savings plan (RRSP) during lower-income years while deferring benefits. Someone expecting substantial RRIF income later might face larger OAS clawbacks even after waiting. Coordinating pension income, registered account withdrawals and income-splitting opportunities can change which starting dates are most tax-efficient. The financial reward for waiting CPP can start at 60, with payments reduced by 36 per cent relative to 65. After 65, payments increase by 0.7 per cent for each month deferred, reaching 42 per cent at 70. OAS can start at 65. Waiting increases payments by 0.6 per cent monthly, or 36 per cent at 70. Neither benefit increases further for deferral beyond 70. Someone entitled to $1,000 monthly in CPP at 65 would receive $1,420 at 70, before future inflation adjustments. The maximum monthly OAS payment for aged 65 to 74 is $762.50 in late 2026. A 36 per cent increase would lift that base payment to approximately $1,037, before indexing. Both benefits are inflation-adjusted, and OAS rises automatically another 10 per cent at 75. How long must you live to come out ahead? Delaying $1,000 monthly in CPP from 65 to 70 means forgoing $60,000, then receiving an additional $420 monthly. On a simple cumulative-payment basis, the higher benefit catches up near age 82. For OAS, the comparable break-even is around age 83, accounting for the 10 per cent increase at 75 applicable to both starting ages. Taxes, inflation, and investment returns can change these results. According to the Office of the Chief Actuary’s 32nd CPP report , a Canadian man aged 65 in 2025 is projected to live another 21.6 years, reaching approximately age 87; for women, the projection is 24.1 years, reaching approximately age 89. These averages cannot predict individual outcomes. Health, lifestyle, and family history should inform longevity assumptions. For those who live into their 90s, higher inflation-adjusted benefits may reduce pressure on portfolios later in life. Individuals eligible for the Guaranteed Income Supplement should generally not defer OAS because doing so delays access to that supplement. A total wealth planning decision There is no universally correct age to begin CPP or OAS. Spouses may benefit from different starting dates, and taking one benefit earlier while deferring the other may make sense. Before deciding, Canadians should prepare or update a comprehensive financial plan that models different scenarios for income needs, tax exposure, portfolio sustainability, and estate objectives. The goal is not simply to collect sooner or secure the largest monthly cheque. It is to make these decisions within a broader total wealth plan that supports after-tax income and lasting financial security. item.title: GSMA urges ‘policy reset’ for Canada’s telecom sector
item.description: A new report says the focus of Canada’s telecommunications policy should shift from lowering consumer prices to creating better conditions to invest.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: TORONTO — A new report says the focus of Canada’s telecommunications policy should shift from lowering consumer prices to creating better conditions for companies to invest in their networks at a time when traditional revenues are plateauing and capital costs are expected to rise. The paper from U.K.-based Global System for Mobile Communications Association calls for a “policy reset” that prioritizes affordable and predictable spectrum pricing, support for 5G and AI infrastructure such as data centres, and improved regulatory certainty. It also recommends continued public-private funding to bolster rural and Indigenous connectivity. “Canada is reaching an inflection point in terms of telecoms policy,” said Niall Magennis, senior policy director for the association, which represents more than 1,000 mobile operators and related businesses across the world. “We have to remember that mobile networks play a key role in the economy.” The report said mobile technologies and services generated 5.4 per cent of Canada’s GDP last year, or roughly US$120 billion of economic value — a figure expected to rise to US$170 billion by 2030, thanks to growing adoption of technologies such as 5G, Internet of Things and AI. But Magennis said much of Canada’s telecommunications policy was crafted in the early 2000s. While some elements were appropriate for decades in a high revenue growth environment, especially as elevated immigration levels brought new customers to Canada, the framework has grown outdated in more recent years. The report pointed to Canada’s immigration slowdown, as telecom operators are now attracting fewer new subscribers and seeing their mobile revenues flatten, despite the rising cost of spectrum licences. “Now the sector is experiencing much more of a squeeze,” said Magennis during a presentation Tuesday in Toronto. Carriers are facing other challenges too. While new cellphone plans have become more affordable for consumers — Magennis noted prices have fallen around 25 per cent over the past two years — telecoms are dealing with cost pressures such as the need to fund the next wave of 5G technology, improve network resiliency, and meet obligations around cybersecurity. Magennis said some operators have also waded into AI, building their own data centres and compute facilities at significant costs.  Without a policy shift, he warned that network quality and innovation could gradually weaken. “We need to be mindful that certain policies have effects on investments,” he said. In recent years, the CRTC has introduced various measures aimed at boosting cellphone and internet competition in Canada, empowering consumers, and lowering costs. The regulator has defended those moves while also acknowledging concerns from carriers, some of whom have announced sizable cuts to their capital investment plans in response to the framework. Speaking at an industry conference this past May, CRTC vice-chairperson Adam Scott said the commission is trying to balance multiple priorities, including “affordable prices alongside investment in high-quality networks and broad network coverage.” “I ... see intense competition putting pressure on top-line revenues and making investment cases more challenging. I see population growth slowing and putting further downward pressure on revenue growth,” said Scott at the time. “The balance is the hard part. Overall, I see a better balance than we’ve had in a long time, but those linkages are real.” Magennis, who planned to present his research to the CRTC and Innovation Science and Economic Development Canada this week, said he agrees on the need to find an equilibrium between those competing priorities. “I don’t think it’s one or the other,” he said. “It’s about finding that balance, finding that right level between maybe some shorter-term concerns and then the longer-term view of ‘What does Canada need?’ An element that needs to be factored into that long-term debate is the need to invest in networks, to be ready for not just 5G now, but ... future network technologies.” --- Sammy Hudes, The Canadian Press This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 20, 2026.
